questions.q: Who is the protagonist in the poem "lk;s esa /wi"? Provide a one-sentence answer based on the text.
questions.a: The protagonist is the first-person speaker ("eSa"), who represents the poet Nagarjun himself as a conscious observer and revolutionary voice. A wrong answer (e.g., "the woods" or "the night") reveals the student cannot distinguish between setting and persona, a fundamental error in poetic analysis.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the protagonist feels restless in the first stanza. What does this restlessness signify about their character?
questions.a: The protagonist's restlessness stems from witnessing the exploitation and hypocrisy of society (the "deceiver" who exploits both home and street). This signifies a deeply empathetic and socially aware character who cannot remain indifferent to injustice. A wrong answer focusing only on physical discomfort (cold, darkness) misses the metaphorical layer and shows literal comprehension only.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "dual address" (the word 'fpjkx' used in two contexts) to analyze the protagonist's view of power. How does this word choice reveal the protagonist's analytical mind?
questions.a: The protagonist uses 'fpjkx' first for the domestic exploiter (landlord/moneylender) and then for the systemic exploiter (state/ruler), showing they see oppression operating at both personal and structural levels. This reveals a character who analyzes power structurally, not just emotionally. A wrong answer that treats both uses as identical misses the progression from micro to macro exploitation.

questions.q: Analyze the three stanzas as three stages of the protagonist's consciousness. What does each stage reveal about their evolving character?
questions.a: Stanza 1: Personal anguish at domestic exploitation (empathetic observer). Stanza 2: Expansion to systemic exploitation (political analyst). Stanza 3: Revolutionary commitment (active resister). Together they show a character moving from feeling to analysis to action. A wrong answer that merely summarizes each stanza's imagery without linking to character development fails the analytical requirement.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the protagonist's final declaration ("rsjk fu”kke gS fly ns ”kqcku 'kk;j dh"). Does it strengthen or weaken their character portrayal? Justify.
questions.a: It strengthens the portrayal by transforming the protagonist from a sufferer into a leader who claims authority ("fu”kke") to speak for the oppressed ("cgj"). The metaphor of giving light ("fly ns") to the dark world ("cgj") shows agency and hope. A wrong answer calling it "arrogant" or "just poetic" fails to evaluate the strategic shift from victimhood to empowerment.

questions.q: Create a two-stanza poem in Hindi (4 lines each) where a similar protagonist observes a modern injustice (e.g., urban displacement, digital divide) and declares resistance. Use the same structural progression: observation → analysis → commitment.
questions.a: A good answer will show: Stanza 1: Concrete imagery of the injustice (e.g., bulldozers, glowing screens). Stanza 2: Identification of the exploiter (builder, algorithm) and declaration of resistance. Poor answers will be generic slogans without imagery or will miss the two-stage progression, revealing inability to transfer the structural pattern.
